  DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether his Ministry has asked Government to consider exemption of 
export duty on certain products like cold rolled coils, for which raw 
materials have been imported under the Advance Licensing Scheme (ALS); 
(b) if so, whether despite export duties announced on various steel 
products, it would be prudent for Government to consider allowing duty-

14 
free export of CR coils, galvanized steel, tubes and pipes, for which HR 
coils have been imported under ALS; 
(c) whether Government has considered roll back of export duty; and 
(d) if so, by when final decision in this regard is likely to be 
taken? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (d) A Statement 
is laid on the Table of the House. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Gireesh Kumar 
Sanghi 

15 
Statement 
(a) During the month of April 2008, Ministry of Steel had taken up the 
issue with Ministry of Finance for devising a scheme for exemption of 
export duty on exports of such steel products, the input material of 
which was being imported under the Advance Authorisation Scheme (AAS) for 
further value addition and exports. This scheme was conceived to achieve 
two objectives; 
(i) To discourage export of domestic steel from being exported out of 
country after further processing and value addition and thereby improve 
domestic steel availability. 
(ii) To facilitate manufacturers with surplus capacity to export value 
added steel products only against import of the corresponding quality 
materials. 
(b) Export duty on hot rolled (HR) coil, cold rolled (CR) coil, pipes 
and tubes etc. was withdrawn with effect from 13.06.2008. Therefore the 
scheme was not implemented. 
(c) and (d) The G overnment has rolled back export duty on all 
categories of steel items, except melting scrap, w.e.f. 31.10.2008. 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Sir, the reply of the hon. Minister states 
that the Government has rolled back export duty on all categories of 
steel items, except melting scrap, w.e.f. 31.10.2008. Sir, my 
supplementary to the hon. Minister is whether the Government is thinking 
in terms of roll back in the import duty on steel and how would the 
Government encourage export of steel from India in the given scenario. 
Sir, in the given scenario, the steel market is going down and 
consumptions are also falling down within the country. Sir, there are 
countries like China whose consumptions are much less than production. 
China consumes about 482 million tonnes of steel, and produces 537 
million tonnes. So, in China, there is a gap of almost 100 million tonnes 
in the consumption and production of steel. It produces about 100 million 
tonnes of extra steel. So, there is likelihood that China would dump 
steel into our country because we are its neighbouring country. So, what 
is the plan of the Government of India in this area?

AIIMS like institutions in the north-east 
*163. SHRI BIRENDRA PRASAD BAISHYA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is planning to include North East Region (NER) 
in its mission of setting up AIIMS like institutions; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, reasons therefor, in so far as AIIMS like institutions 
will solve the problems of entire NER? 

19 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) 
to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
Statement 
North Eastern Indira Gandhi Regional Institute of Health & Medical 
Sciences (NEIGRIHMS) has been established in Shillong, on the lines of 
AIIMS, New Delhi, and PGIMER, Chandigarh, with the objective  of  
providing advanced specialized Health- Care to the people of North- East 
Region. So far  

20 
Central Government has made an investment of about Rs.400 crores for 
development of the institute. An amount of Rs. 1266.38 crore has been 
allocated for the Institute in the XIth Plan. The Institute is planned 
for a 500 bed referral hospital with 35 teaching departments at post-
graduate level in various specialties and super- specialties. A 50 seat 
Nursing College and Undergraduate MBBS College has already started 
functioning from the Institute. During the year 2008- 09, Rs.59 crore has 
been allocated, of which an amount of Rs. 15 crore has been released. A 
new Regional Cancer Centre, with a 100- bed Cancer Hospital is also 
planned at the Institute. 
Regional Institute of Medical Science, Imphal, has been taken over by 
the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare from NEC in 2008. The Institute 
has an intake capacity of 100 undergraduate and 73, postgraduate 
Degree/Diploma seats. For the development of the Institute as a Centre of 
Excellence, an amount of Rs. 589.92 crore has been allocated for the XIth 
Plan. During the year 2008-09, Rs. 65 crore has been allocated, of which 
an amount of Rs. 48.39 crore has been released. 
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has also taken over the 
Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoli Regional Institute of Mental Health (LGBRIMH), 
Tezpur, and Regional Institute of Paramedical and Nursing Sciences 
(RIPANS), Aizwal, from NEC in 2008. These institutions have been 
allocated an amount of Rs. 267.07 crore and Rs. 69.62 crore respectively 
in the XIth Plan for their overall development as Centres of Excellence 
in their respective fields. During the year 2008-09, Rs. 31 crore and Rs. 
14 crore has been respectively allocated to these Institutions, of which 
an amount of Rs.24.50 crore and Rs. 7.25 crore have been released.  
The upgrdation of Gauhati Medical College, Guwahati, at a total cost 
of Rs. l19.95 crore has also been approved. In addition, a sum of Rs.10 
crore has been released for upgradation of Regional Institute of 
Ophthalmology at Guwahati Medical College. 
The proposal for upgradation of State Civil Hospital at Naharlagun, 
Arunachal Pradesh, at an estimated cost of Rs. l30 crore has also been 
agreed to by the Planning Commission and Detailed Project Report is being 
prepared by Hospital Services Consultancy Corporation Ltd. (HSCC). 

21 
2 new Nursing Colleges and 14 new Nursing Schools have also been 
sanctioned under National Rural Health Mission. Apart from this, under 
National Rural Health Mission (NRHM), as part of the process of 
strengthening all District Hospitals, financial assistance has been 
provided for upgradation of 75 District Hospitals in the North Eastern 
States. Community Health Centres (CHC) are also being upgraded to 30- 50 
bedded hospitals conforming to the norms called 'Indian Public Health 
Standards (IPHS)' in the North Eastern States. 
North Eastern Institute of Folk Medicine (NEIFM) at Pasighat, 
Arunachal Pradesh, has been approved under Department of AYUSH, at an 
estimated cost of Rs.32.88 crore and North Eastern Institute of Ayurveda 
and Homoeopathy (NEIAH) at Shillong, Meghalaya,  has also been approved 
at  

22 
NEIGRIHMS, Shillong, at an estimated cost of Rs. 67.51 crore. 
SHRI BIRENDRA PRASAD BAISHYA: Sir, decentralisation of the pattern of 
medical treatment is the call of the hour. If yo u look at the slogan of 
2008 they have said, "Health for All". The decision of setting up six 
AIIMS like hospitals at Raipur, Bhopal, Patna, Rishikesh, Bhubaneswar, 
etc. taken by the Government was a dynamic one. But it is difficult for 
me to understand why North- Eastern Region, which includes eight States, 
Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura, etc., is deleted from this 
scheme. Sir, although the hon. Minister has categorically stated in his 
reply that the North- Eastern Indira Gandhi Regional Institute of Health 
and Medical Sciences is established in Shillong, on the lines of AIIMS, 
New Delhi and PGIMER, Chandigarh, but, Sir, I would like to mention here 
that this Institute was established in 1987 and the decision of setting 
up of six AIIMS like hospitals was taken in 2003. So my specific question 
is why the Government is neglecting the North -Eastern Region and is 
depriving crores of people of North- Eastern Region from better medical 
treatment. 
DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS: Sir, the Government is definitely not neglecting 
the North Eastern Region on health care and we have a good institution 
called NEIGRIMS, i.e. North Eastern Indira Gandhi Regional Institution of 
Health and Medical Sciences in Meghalaya. Even though it took us quite 
some time to complete this process of construction and functioning of 
hospital, in fact, the foundation stone was laid by late Shri Rajiv 
Gandhi at that point of time and since then there was a long process of 
construction because of some problems associated with that region and 
because some contractors were killed and there were other issues involved 
which I don't want to dwell on. Nevertheless, it is a shining example of 
the commitment of the Government of India for the North- East and that 
institute is a very, very beautiful institution which is envisaged to be 
a 500-bedded hospital. Already it is functioning with 430 beds with 30 to 
35 specialities, including all these services. Also we are going to 
construct a new 100- bedded cancer hospital in that campus itself plus a 
North-Eastern Ayurvedic and Homeopathic college is supposed to come 
there. Nursing college is also functional, medical college is also 
functional there. I would urge upon the Members of Parliament to go there 
and visit that institution and see. The Health Ministry can coordinate 
the process of your visiting and give us more inputs on that. Sir, hon. 
Member said that they have been setting up six new AIIMS like 

23 
institutions, in places which are in low indices of health, in States 
like Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Madhya Pradesh, 
Bhubaneswar and Jodhpur in Rajasthan. Coming back to the point raised by 
hon. Member that North-East has been neglected, I would say, definitely, 
it is not. The Regional Institute of Medical Sciences is in Imphal now. 
The Health Ministry has taken over it. Now you can see my reply which 
says that nearly an amount of about Rs. 589 crores has been allocated for 
that institution for the Eleventh Plan and we are trying to improve that 
facility on par with AIIMS like institution as well plus also the 
Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoloi Institute of Mental Health, Tejpur. That is 
also being taken over by the Government of India, Health Ministry and 
that has a Plan amount of approximately Rs. 267 crores which we are going 
to invest in that plus we have upgraded some of the Government medical 
colleges and in the first phase we have taken up the Guwahati Medical 
College at a cost of approximately Rs. 120 crores which is going to be 
upgraded. Some of them have been already earmarked for that as well. Some 
of the other institutions are like the proposed upgradation of State 
Civil Hospital in Nawalgarh in Arunachal Pradesh at an estimated cost of 
approximately Rs. 130 crores. Under the National Rural Health Mission all 
the district headquarter hospitals are being upgraded. All of them are 
being upgraded. There are about 87 district headquarter hospitals. All 
the community health centres, all the primary health centres, all the 
sub-centres in the entire North- Eastern Region are being upgraded under 
the National Rural Health Mission. 
SHRI BIRENDRA PRASAD BAISHYA: Sir, I am thankful to the hon. Minister. 
In his statement he categorically said he has given money to the Regional 
Institute of Medical Sciences, Imphal. They have given money to some 
civil hospital. But, Sir, my question is quite specific. My question was 
that of AIIMS like hospital and hon. Minister said, we took the step of 
opening such hospitals in only those regions which are medically 
backward. But it is known to everybody that the entire North- Eastern 
Region is totally backward when we compare with the other parts of the 
country. I have nothing to say about Rishikesh. I have nothing to say 
against Bhopal. I have nothing to say anything against Bhubaneswar. But, 
Sir, the distance from Delhi to Bhopal is just eight hours; the distance 
from Delhi to Raipur is only eight hours. The distance from Delhi to 
Rishkesh is just five hours but the distance from Delhi to North- Eastern 
Region is more than 2000 kilometers and infrastrutural development of the 
North-Eastern Region is yet to be developed. Also, during floods, the 

24 
entire North- Eastern Region is totally cut off with the rest of the 
country. In such a situation, it is impossible for any person to go to 
Delhi or any other part of the country for a better and urgent medical 
treatment. In view of this, and Guwahati being the heart of the North-
East, will the hon. Minister seriously consider setting up of an AIIMS-
like institution in Guwahati. 
DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS: Sir, the aim of the Government is that not a 
single patient from the North- East should go out of North- East for 
treatment due to lack of medical facilities there. We are prioritising 
facilities in the North-East in a very big way. I have already mentioned 
some of the things that we have initiated. There are also other 
facilities which we are putting in there. Our aim is that no patient from 
the North- East should go out of North- East for treatment and we are 
providing every medical facility there itself. On these lines, the 
NEIGRIHMS in the North- East is an AIIMS- like institution. That is why, 
when it was planned for setting up of six new AIIMS-like institutions, it 
was not planned for the North- East as it is already having an AIIMS- like 
institution. In fact, the NEIGRIHMS is bigger than what is planned in the 
six States. And, we are planning to further expand it. I hope the hon. 
Member would be satisfied with this reply.

CAG report on railways 
*167. DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
 SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE : 
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether CAG has rapped the Railways for irregularities, poor 
planning and deficiencies in stores and contract management and pointed 
out a loss of Rs 801 crore during nine months, as Railway Board had fixed 
haulage rates recoverable for container traffic on Container Corporation 
of India Limited (CONCOR) at less than the base rates; 
(b) if so, whether the report also contradicts his statement that his 
Ministry is showing profit, as actually it is running in losses; and 
(c) if so, what are the other main points mentioned in the audit 
report and what are the steps being taken to implement the suggestions 
made by the CAG? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) to (c) The Report of 
CAG for the year ending March 2007 has mentioned inter- alia certain 
deficiencies in stores and contract management and fixing of haulage 
charges for containers. The Report was laid on the Table of the House on 

39 
24th October, 2008. The other main points contained in the Audit Report 
relate to financial management, earnings, works and assets management. 
The observations of the audit are examined in detail as per laid down 
procedure and time frame and Action Taken Note where required are 
submitted to Public Accounts Committee duly vetted by the CAG's office 
through Ministry of Finance. The Report does not contradict that Indian 
Railways have been generating surplus during this period. The basis on 
which the losses have been worked out in case of container traffic by 
Audit is actually not applicable for this traffic. The principle of 
rating for haulage charges for container is different than the principle 
of rating of freight charges for railway wagons where alone the base rate 
concept is relevant. In case of containers, haulage charges are levied 
separately for loaded and empty wagons and are based on fully distributed 
costs with a margin of profit over the cost of operation thus arrived at. 
Indian Railways do not incur losses on container movement.

(c) if so, whether in the GoM meeting held in April, 2008, no decision

on drugs which has been interpreted as per Supreme Court Order; 
(d) if so, the steps Government proposes to take; and 
(e) by when a final decision in this regard is likely to be taken? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) 
The Draft National Pharmaceuticals Policy was submitted before the 
Cabinet for its approval. The Cabinet considered the Policy in its 
meeting held on 11- 1-2007 and decided that the matter may, in the first 
instance, be considered by a Group of Ministers (GOM). GOM has since been 
constituted and has held four meetings so far on 10.4.2007, 12.9.2007, 
30.1.2008 and 30.4.2008. GOM is yet to make its recommendations to the

Amendment of PC and PNDT Act 
*176. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 

54 
(a) whether Government is aware that sex determination tests are being 
conducted by doctors at several medical centres/hospitals illegally in 
the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the Pre- conception (PC) and Pre- natal Diagnostic 
Techniques (PNDT) Act has completely failed to check the rising cases of 
its violation; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
(e) whether Government proposes to amend the PC and PNDT Act to make 
it stringent; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) 
to (f) Sex determination techniques have been in use in India since 1975 
primarily for the determination of genetic abnormalities. However, these 
techniques were widely misused to determine the sex of the foetus and 
subsequent abortions if the foetus was found to be female. 
Studies indicate that sex determination tests are conducted and female 
foeticide carried out surreptitiously with the active connivance of the 
service providers and the persons seeking such services. Unlike in other 
cases, both parties gain through such complicity, i.e. while the service 
seekers are able to get rid of the unwanted female foetus, the service 
providers benefit financially. The absence of witness to such unholy 
alliance or evidence thereto makes it difficult to detect violations of 
the Act. 
With a view to overcoming such circumvention of the law, the 
implementing agencies, as also the NGOs and other organisations, are 
encouraged to employ decoy customers for trapping such unscrupulous 
service providers and book cases against them under the law. 
Further, the Government has taken action on strengthening the Pre -
Conception & Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act (PC & PNDT Act) as well 
as creating awareness on the issue through various IEC mechanisms. Some 
of the steps taken by the Government to improve the Child Sex Ratio in 
the Country are: 
• Constitution of the Central Supervisory Board under the Chairmanship 
of Union Minister of Health & Family Welfare, whose function, inter 
alia, is to advise the Central Government on policy matters relating 
to use of pre- natal diagnostic techniques, sex selection techniques 
and against their misuse and to create public awareness against the 
practice of pre- conception sex selection and pre- natal determination 

55 
of sex of foetus leading to female foeticide; 
• Constitution of the National Inspection & Monitoring Committee (NIMC) 
for undertaking field visits periodically across the country. 
• Constitution of the National Support & Monitoring Cell (NSMC) for 
effective implementation of the Act. 
• The reports of NIMC and NSMC are forwarded to the concerned State/UT 
Governments with the request to take appropriate remedial action for 
plugging any shortcomings, including initiation of penal proceedings 
against the violators pointed out in the reports, since implementation 
of the Act rests with the State/UT Governments. 

56 
• Provisions have also been made for sensitising Judiciary and public 
prosecutors. 
• Publication of Annual Reports, Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs). 
• On-Line Complaint registration facility on the Ministry's Website. 
• Organising sensitisation workshops/ seminars, launching of 'Save the 
Girl Child' campaign, seeking cooperation from the NGOs/religious 
leaders, etc. 
• Further, under the National Rural Health Mission, Auxiliary Nursing 
Midwife (ANM) and Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) are being 
sensitised on the issue. Also, funds have been provided to all 
States/UTs under the Rural Child Health programme for implementation 
of the Act and related activities. 
• Steps are also afoot to further strengthen the PC & PNDT Act, 1994 and 
the Rules framed thereunder in consultation with the legal experts and 
all the stake holders. It is proposed to amend the Act suitably with a 
view to making penalty provisions for violators of the Act more 
stringent, including imposition of fine up to Rs.5 lakhs and 
incarceration up to 1 years upon conviction, is being considered in 
consultation with legal experts and all the stake holders.

*178. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of

sufficiency in foodgrains, the country will be a chronic importer of

additional 20 million tonnes of foodgrains (rice 10 million tonnes, wheat

tonnes of rice, 8 million tonnes of wheat and 2 million tonnes of pulses

of Soil Health & Fertility in November, 2008 to promote balanced use of

was also launched in 2007 -08 with an outlay of Rs. 25000 crores for XI 
Plan (2007-08 to 2011- 12) to incentivise States to invest and reorient 
the current agricultural development strategies. 
Although it would be too early to predict about the food situation in 
2020, it can be visualized with a reasonable degree of confidence that 
the country would not only remain comfortable on foodgrains front during 
the 11th Plan but may also have some elbow room for export of wheat and 
rice.

farming, e- trading etc. The progress of the amendment of the State 
Agricultural Produce Marketing Committee (APMC) Act is given in the 
Statement (See below). 
To facilitate the implementation of amended provisions, the Ministry 
of Agriculture has also formulated Model APMC Rules and circulated to the 
States/Union Territories for adoption in November, 2007. Chapter IX of 
the Model APMC Rules provide provisions for Establishment and Functioning 
of Private Market Yard/Private Market/Private E- Market, Consumer/Farmer 
Market and Direct purchase. So far, the State Governments of Andhra 
Pradesh, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Orissa, Himachal Pradesh and Karnataka 
have notified their amended APMC Rules, whereas Madhya Pradesh and 
Haryana have partially amended the Rules.

Crop damage due to insect 
1245. SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: 
 SHRI KAMAL AKHTAR: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 

70 
(a) whether it is a fact that rice crop in East Asia is being damaged 
by an insect known as the Brown Plant Hopper, which is multiplying by the 
billions and chewing rice paddy thus threatening diets of poor people; 
(b) whether Government has examined the possibility of the insect 
reaching India and damaging the rice crops in the country; and 
(c) if so, the steps being taken to address the problem? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTI LAL 
BHURIA): (a) and (b) The Brown Plant Hopper is an insect pest of paddy in 
the rice growing countries of East Asia. As per survey reports received 
from State Departments of Agriculture and the Central Integrated Pest 
Management Centres (CIPMCs), trace to moderate incidence of Brown Plant 
Hopper has been reported from isolated fields of Kerala State and 
moderate to severe incidence of Brown Plant Hopper has been reported from 
Haryana State. 
(c) Experts from Government of India have already visited the affected 
areas in Haryana. Presently, the insect is under control. The Government 
of India has adopted Integrated Pest Management (IPM) as the main 
strategy for plant protection, including paddy crop. Awareness for pest 
control through IPM approach is spread among the farmers under the scheme 
"Strengthening and Modernization of Pest Management Approach in India" 
through Farmers' Field Schools organized by 31 CIPMs across the country.

Permission to farmers for selling agricultural products in any market 
†1250. MISS ANUSUIYA UIKEY: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government has allowed farmers to sell 
their agricultural produce in any market of the country; 
(b) if so, whether the farmers of border districts of Madhya Pradesh 
could sell sugarcane and jaggery in the districts of Maharashtra; and 
(c) the reasons for which the farmers of Madhya Pradesh cannot sell 
their produce in Maharashtra? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTI LAL 
BHURIA): (a) Yes, Sir. For providing better market access opportunities, 
the Ministry of Agriculture had drafted a Model Act titled "The 
agricultural Produce Marketing (Development and Regulation) Act, 2003" in 
consultation with the State Governments for amendment of the States APMC 
Act. The Model Act contains provisions such as removal of compulsion on 
growers to sell their produce through existing regulated markets, 
prohibition of commission agency, rationalization of market fees, 
allowing establishment of direct purchase centers and Farmers Markets for 
direct sale, enabling any person/grower or local authority to establish 
new markets in any area, professionalization of management of markets, 
promotion of Public Private Partnership in management and development of 
markets, promotion of contract farming etc. Besides this, the Government 
of India has also amended the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 removing 
restrictions on the storage and movement of goods and permitted futures 
trading in number of Agricultural Commodities for better market access 
opportunities for farmers. As such there is no ban for farmers to sell 
their agricultural produce in any market of the country under the States 
APMC Act. 
(b) As of date, jaggery has not been notified under the Madhya Pradesh 
Krishi Upaj Mandi Adhiniyam, 1972 and sugarcane has been exempted from 
the purview of payment of mandi fee by the State Government. Madhya 
Pradesh Krishi Upaj Mandi Adhiniyam, 1972 does not provide for imposing 
restrictions on sale of notified agricultural commodities outside the 
State or within the State.

†1280. SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi 

127 
(a) whether it is a fact that inspite of having almost same 
ingredients, different pharmaceutical companies are selling their drugs 
at different rates by using their brand names; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that doctors prescribe costly branded 
drugs in order to get more commission, which causes exploitation of 
patients; and

generic name instead of brand names? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) 
Under the provisions of the Drugs (Price Control) Order, 1995, the prices 
of 74 bulk drugs and the formulations containing any of these scheduled 
drugs are controlled. The Government / NPPA fixes / revises their prices 
from time to time as per formula provided under DPCO. 
As per the DPCO '95 every manufacturer or importer shall carry into 
effect the price of a bulk drugs or formulation as the case may be, as 
fixed by the Government from time to time, within fifteen days from the 
date of notification in the official Gazette or receipt of the order of 
the Government in this behalf by such manufacturer or importer. 
In respect of drugs, which are not covered under prices control (non-
scheduled formulations), the manufacturers are free to fix the prices by 
themselves without seeking approval of Government / NPPA. Prices of Non-
Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturer themselves 
considering the various factors like cost of production, marketing/ 
selling expenses, R & D expenses, trade commission, market competition, 
product innovation, product quality etc. In some cases it is observed 
that companies are selling different brands at different rates. There is 
no provision in DPCO, 95 to restrict different prices for different 
brands in case of non-scheduled formulations.

medicines instead of branded medicines. In this directions Government has 
decided to open "Jan Aushadhi" generic drug stores in the country

instead of brand names. Government has already inaugurated a 'Jan 
Aushadhi' generic drug store at civil hospital, Amritsar on 25.11.2008.

Will the Minister of CHEMICAILS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi 

131 
(a) whether various companies engaged in manufacturing of pesticides 
are using dangerous chemicals; 
(b) whether any investigation is made from time to time about the 
safety measures adopted in these companies by Government, so that a 
situation like Bhopal gas tragedy may not arise; 
(c) whether a company in Faridabad near Delhi engaged in pesticide 
manufacturing is using dangerous chemicals without any licence and 
employees have given a memorandum to Assistant Director, Industrial 
Safety and Health and Chemicals in this regard; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS 
(SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) and (b) Pesticides are used to control pests 
and insects and therefore, inherently hazardous. Since several hazardous 
chemicals are used in manufacturing of different kinds of pesticides, 
safety measures to be adopted are in- built in the provisions of the 
Insecticides Act, 1968 and the Rules framed there under. Department of 
Agriculture and Cooperation, Ministry of Agriculture is the Nodal 
Department for this Act. Registration with the Registration Committee, 
constituted under the Act is a pre-requisite for import or manufacture of 
insecticides (pesticides). The Registration Committee has prescribed 
minimum infrastructure facilities for the companies engaged in 
manufacture of insecticides. After registration, a license to manufacture 
insecticide has to be obtained from the Licensing Officer of the 
respective State where the insecticide is proposed to be manufactured. 
The Licensing Officer is required to inspect the manufacturing premises 
and ensure availability of minimum infrastructure facilities for 
manufacture of insecticides for which a manufacturer is obtaining the 
manufacturing license. Minimum infrastructure facilities include 
reasonable premises, requisite plant and machinery, protective clothing, 
equipment, including respiratory devices and other facilities for workers 
including first-aid measures as well as availability of antidotes. The 
manufacturers are also required to arrange suitable training in observing 
safety precautions and handling safety equipments provided to them. All 
the persons who are engaged in the work of handling, dealing or otherwise 
coming in contact with the insecticides during their manufacture or 
formulation are required to be periodically medically examined by a 
qualified doctor. 
(c) and (d) There is no such report available with the Department of 
Agriculture & Cooperation, Government of India which is the 
administrative Department for the Insecticides Act. Implementation of the 
Insecticides Act including the licensing, falls under the purview of the

Compensation to Bhopal tragedy victims 
1286. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of compensation paid so far by the Union Carbide 
factory in Bhopal owned by DOW Chemicals which leaked 27 tonnes of lethal 
gas over the city during 1984 causing death of thousands of people, 
leaving several thousands as orphans and crippled who drink poisonous 
polluted drinking water daily, even after nearly 25 years after that 
disaster, and remedial measures taken so-far; 
(b) whether DOW Chemicals Public Affairs Specialist Kathy Hunt said 
during 2002 that 500 dollars as compensation for an Indian victim of that 
gas tragedy was plenty amount while justifying in having paid 10 million 
dollars to an American child who suffered brain damage caused by its 
Dursban Insecticide Factory; and 
(c) if so, the action taken in this regard towards payment of 
compensation to every crippled victim of Bhopal Gas Tragedy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS 
(SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) The process of distribution of compensation to 
gas victims commenced in 1992 and 10,29,517 claim cases were filed for 
compensation.All the cases have since been settled. As on 30- 11-2008, 
compensation of Rs. 1548.95 crore has been awarded to 5,73,856 claimants 
of the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster, found to be eligible by the Welfare 
Commissioner, who is a sitting judge of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh. 
In addition to this, in compliance with the orders of the Supreme Court 
dated 19th July 2004, and 26th October 2004, pro-rata compensation on 1:1 
basis of Rs. 1509.13 crore has been disbursed among 5,62,388 claimants, 
till 07.11.2008. 
The various relief and rehabilitation works undertaken, so far are as 
follows: 
Under the medical rehabilitation plan, 7 hospitals, 5 civil 
dispensaries and 2 poly clinics and 3 dispensaries each of the 
Homeopathy, Unani and Indian Medical Systems are engaged in the medical 
care and treatment of the victims residing in 36 gas affected wards of 
Bhopal. In addition, 3 more hospitals consisting one each of Ayurveda, 
Homeopathy and Unani System of medicines are also functioning. The Indian 
Council of Medical Research (ICMR) had taken up 24 studies to evaluate 

145 
the effects of MIC gas on the victims. The ICMR closed its research work 
in 1993-94 and the team of Scientists engaged in this work had continued 
to work under the State Government. The Central Government had provided a 
Corpus Fund of Rs.5 crore to continue this work. 
Under the economic rehabilitation, training was provided to the youth 
of gas affected wards, 42 work- sheds and 152 industrial sheds were 
constructed for providing employment opportunities in the Units set up in 
these sheds. 

146 
Under the social rehabilitation plan, 2468 houses were constructed and 
allotted to the widows of the gas victims besides providing initial 
relief measures like pensions to about 1077 widows, distribution of milk 
to the lactating mothers and the children, etc. 
Under the environmental rehabilitation, construction of drains, 
plantation of trees and augmentation of safe drinking water supply was 
taken up. In April, 2006, Government of India had sanctioned money for a 
project under the Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission 
(JNNURM) and the Government of Madhya Pradesh had sanctioned Rs.14.18 
crore to the Bhopal Municipal Corporation (BMC) for providing safe 
drinking water through pipelines from the Kolar Reservoir to the 14 
localities around the UCIL plant site. The Government of Madhya Pradesh 
is implementing the Scheme. 
(b) The Government of India has no information in the matter. 
(c) The details have been given in the reply to (a) above.

Fortified and coated fertilizer 
1290. SHRI JESUDASU SEELAM: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in view of rising fertilizers subsidy bill, Government has 
decided to put entire burden of additional secondary and micro- nutrients 
required to help to counter imbalanced fertilizers use in country on 
farmers; 
(b) if so, whether Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs which met 
under Chairmanship of PM approved a policy for encouraging production and 
availability of fortified and coated fertilizers; 
(c) if so, whether under the policy, manufacturer will be allowed to 
sell fertilizers coated or fortified with secondary or micro-nutrients up 
to a maximum of 5 per cent above notified maximum retail price for all 
fertilizers under fertilizer control order; and 
(d) to what extent it will be helpful to both the farmer and to the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS 
(SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) to (d) The Cabinet Committee on Economic 
Affairs has approved a new policy for fortified/coated fertilizers with 
the objective to promote its production and application within the 
country. The application of secondary and micro- nutrients along with the 
primary nutrients is expected to promote balanced fertilization and lead 
to increased agricultural productivity. Under the new policy, the 
manufacturer is allowed to charge upto 5% more than the MRP in case of 
fortified/coated subsidized fertilizers except for Zincated Urea and 
Boronatecl SSP, for which the manufacturer is allowed a ceiling of 10% 
above MRP of Urea and SSP respectively. 
The farmer is free to make its own rational decision based on crop and 
soil requirement as to whether the fortification/coating with secondary 
and micro- nutrients at an additional cost is going to provide an 
additional productivity leading to larger gain to the farmer. Moreover, 
the price band above MRP is also expected to breed competition amongst 
manufacturers to provide better fertilizer products to the farmers. 

156

(a) whether it is a fact that there has not been much investment in 
fertilizers sector during the last 10 year, because the potential 
investors wanted Government to decontrol the sector and direct subsidy 
payment to the farmers; 
(b) if so, whether industry's demand has been fully examined by the 
Abhijit Sen Committee which is looking into all the option for attracting 
investment in urea business; 
(c) whether Government has reportedly taken any decision on 7th 
August, 2008 regarding New Fertilizers Investment Policy; and 
(d) if so, what are the salient features thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS 
(SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) to (d) The Government had announced in January 
2004 a policy based on cost plus approach with urea price derived on the 
principle of Long Run Average Cost (LRAC) for expansion of a unit and 
setting up of a Greenfield project. This policy was not successful in 
attracting investment in this sector. In view of the imminent need of a 
New Investment Policy for urea sector, a proposal based on IPP benchmark 
was placed before the GOM constituted to look into sustainable use of 
fertilizers and pertinent subsidy and pricing issue. The GOM constituted 
a Committee under the Chairmanship of Prof. Abhijit Sen. The Committee 
examined all the options and based on the recommendations of Committee, 
the Government has announced a policy for new investments in urea sector 
on 4th September 2008. The New Investment Policy aims at revamp, 
expansion, revival of existing urea units and setting up of Greenfield 
projects. The policy aims at bridging the gap in next five years between 
the consumption and domestic production subject to confirmed and adequate 
availability of gas at reasonable prices. The salient features of the new 
investment policy are as under :- 
1. The policy is based on Import Parity Price(IPP) benchmark with 

158 
suitable floor and ceiling prices. 
2. Floor & Ceiling prices: The floor for urea price is be kept at USD 250 
per MT and the ceiling for urea price is fixed at USD 425 per MT. 
3. Revamp project: Any improvement in capacity of existing plants through 
investment upto Rs. 1000 crore, in the existing train of ammonia- urea 
production will be treated as revamp of existing units.  The  
additional  urea from the revamp of existing units will be recognized 
at 85% of Import  

159 
Parity Price with the floor and ceiling price as indicated above. 
4. Expansion projects: Setting up of a new ammonia-urea plant (a separate 
new ammonia-urea train) in the premises of the existing fertilizer 
plants, utilizing some of the common utilities will qualify for being 
treated as expansion project. The investment should exceed a minimum  
limit of Rs.3000 crore. The urea from the expansion of existing units 
will be recognized at 90% of IPP, with the floor and ceiling price as 
indicated above. 
5. Revival/Brownfield projects: The urea from the revived units of 
Hindustan Fertilizer Corporation Limited(HFCL) and Fertilizer 
Corporation of India Limited (FCIL) will be recognized at 95% of IPP 
with prescribed floor & ceiling price, if the revival of closed units 
takes placed in public sector. 
6. Greenfield projects: The pricing of Greenfield projects will be 
decided based on a bidding process which will be for a discount over 
IPP, after firming up of the location (States) of the proposed new 
plants. 
7. Gas transportation charges: An additional gas transportation cost will 
be paid to units undertaking expansion and revival on the basis of 
actuals (upto 5.2 Gcal per MT of urea) as decided by the 
Regulator(Gas) subject to a maximum ceiling of USD 25 per MT of urea. 
8. Allocation of Gas: Only non- APM gas will be considered for the new 
investment in urea sector. 
9. Coal gasification based Urea Projects: The Coal gasification based 
urea projects will also be treated on par with a revival or a 
Greenfield project as the case may be. In addition, any other 
incentives or tax benefits as provided by Government for encouraging 
coal gasification technology will also be extended to these projects. 
10. Joint Ventures abroad: The Joint Venture projects abroad in gas 
rich countries are also proposed to be encouraged through firm offtake 
contracts with pricing decided on the basis of prevailing market 
conditions and in mutual consultation with the joint venture company. 
However, the principle for deciding upon the maximum price will be the 
price achieved under Greenfield projects or 95% of IPP as proposed for 
revival projects (in absence of any Greenfield projects) with a cap of 
USD 405 CIF India per MT and a floor of USD 225 CIF India per MT 
(inclusive of handling and bagging costs). 
11. Time period for proposed investment policy: Only those revamp 
projects which start production of additional capacities within four 
years of notification of the new policy would qualify for the 

160 
dispensation recommended above. Similarly production from expansion 
and revival (brownfield) units that come about within five years of 
notification of the new policy would qualify for dispensation provided 
in the policy. If the production does not come through within the 
stipulated time period, such brownfield projects will be treated 
similar to a Greenfield projects wherein price will be decided through 
limited bidding options. The time period for setting up of new Joint 
Ventures would also be five years under the new investment policy.

Statement-II 
Scheme for distribution of subsidised imported edible oils  
through State Governments/UTs 
1. The Scheme for distribution of subsidized edible oils would be 
restricted to imported edible oils. PSUs may import refined 
palmolein/soyabean oil for the initial two months to facilitate 
implementation of the Scheme without delay and thereafter crude 
palm/soya oil may also be imported. 
2. PSUs viz. PEC, MMTC, STC and NAFED will import edible oils under the 
Scheme and PEC will coordinate with other PSUs in all the matters 
relating the import, refining and supplying the packed edible oils to 
the State Governments. 
3. The subsidy would be limited to Rs. 15 per kg. of imported oil. The 
subsidy would be given to the PSUs directly by the Government of 
India. 
4. The PSUs would supply the subsidized oil to State Governments/UTs who 
will supply the oil to ration card holders. The maximum quantity so 
distributed by State Governments will not exceed 1 kg. of edible oil 
per ration card/family per month. They may distribute the subsidized 
oil through PDS shops/other outlets as decided by them. They may 
restrict the distribution to BPL families or cover a part of the APL 
families as well depending upon the availability and the distribution 
logistics. It would be the responsibility of the State Government to 
ensure that the oil is not diverted/leaked and the targeted consumers 
get it. 
5. The State Governments would decide the price at which the oil would be 
sold to the ration card holders. The State Governments will pass on 
the entire subsidy to the ration card holders. 
6. The refined oil would be packed in packets of 1 kg./l/2 kg as desired 
by the State Governments with a label mentioning that it is subsidized 
by the Government of India alongwith other relevant details. 
7. The State Governments/UTs would place their demands, restricted to 
allocation made by the Government of India, with the PSUs and lift the 
stocks within the time agreed upon. The State Governments would take 
delivery of the refined oil from the PSUs delivery point/packing 
centre. 
8. The State Governments would be charged the entire cost of import upto 
packing and transport, including charges incurred by PSUs such as port 
charges, bank charges, trading margin, etc. minus the subsidy @ Rs. 
15/- per kg. The cost of transportation from the packing 

199 
centre/distribution centre and all other costs will be borne by the 
States/UTs concerned. The PSUs will intimate the modalities for 
payment and other financial transactions to the State Governments. 
9. Trading margin (administrative cost) upto a maximum of 0.75% of the 
landed cost of oil and other costs such as port charges, refining and 
packing may be charged by the PSUs. This will, however, be subsumed in 
the subsidy mentioned in para 8 above. 
10. The subsidies from GOI will be restricted to a total one million 
tonnes of edible oil under this Scheme during financial year 2008-09. 
However, initially 3 lakh tonnes of oil will be allocated amongst the 
States. 

200 
11. The edible oil will be allocated by the Department of Food & 
Public Distribution to the States taking into account the BPL 
population of the State, the quantity requested for allocation under 
this Scheme by the States, efficient distribution mechanism put in 
place by the S tate Government for this purpose and prompt offtake of 
subsidized edible oil by the States. 
12. In case of States not lifting the allocated edible oil within one 
month of allocation, the allocation to such States shall stand 
cancelled and the quantity shall be reallocated to other States. 
13. The States shall give monthly Statement to the Government of India 
mentioning the: 
 i. Quantity lifted by them; 
 ii. Quantity distributed through PDS mechanism; and 
 iii. Price at which such oil has been distributed. 
14. This Scheme will initially be implemented for 3 months and can be 
extended after a review is done of its impact on domestic availability 
and prices of edible oils.

utilize this stock and avoid losses due to damage to quality of

(ii) Adequate dunnage material, fumigation covers and chemicals are

properly covered with specifically fabricated low density black 
polythene water proof covers and tied with nylon ropes/nets.

Statement-III 
Details of schemes to improve the health status of children and women 
The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM), (2005- 2012), and under its 
umbrella, the Reproductive and Child Health Programme Phase II, launched 
by the Government of India in the year 2005, aims to improve access to 
equitable, affordable, accountable and effective primary health care, in 
the rural areas of the country, especially for poor women and children, 
with a special focus on 18 States which have weak public health 
indicators and weak infrastructure and to improve the health status of 
children and women and to bring down the child and maternal mortality 
rate. The interventions being implemented under this programme are as 

216 
follows: 
• Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), a cash benefit scheme to promote 
Institutional Delivery with a special focus on Below Poverty Line 
(BPL) and SC/ST pregnant women; 

217 
• Appointment of an Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) for every 
village to facilitate accessing of health care services by the 
community including pregnant women; 
• Operationalising Community Health Centers as First Referral Units 
(FRUs) and 50% of all Primary Health Centers for providing 24X7 
services. 
• Augmenting the availability of skilled manpower by means of different 
skill-based trainings such as for providing Skilled Attendance at 
Birth. 
• Training of MBBS Doctors in Life Saving Anesthetic Skills and 
Emergency Obstetric Care including Caesarian Section; 
• Strengthening of District Hospitals, Community Health Centres, Primary 
Health Care centres and Sub- centres to provide basic essential 
maternal and child health care. 
• Provision of 24 hours service in Primary Health Care centres and 
Skilled Attendance at Birth. 
• Strengthening of CHCs for first referral care - Provision of Emergency 
Obstetric and Neonatal Care at FRUs & Training of MBBS Doctors in Life 
Saving Anesthetics Skills for Emergency Obstertric Care. 
• Supplementary nutrition to pregnant and lactating mothers. 
• National nutrition anaemia prophylaxis programme. 
• Essential newborn care (care at birth – protection from hypothermia – 
provision of warmth, cord care -  protection from infection, early 
initiation of breastfeeding). 
• Immunisation. 
• Infant and young Child Feeding (Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months & 
timely introduction of complimentary feeding). 
• Vitamin A supplementation. 
• Iron and Folic Acid supplementation. 
• Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI), early 
detection and appropriate management of Acute Respiratory Infection 
(ARI), Diarrhoea and other infections among new born and under five 
children. 
Shortage of health workers 
1318. SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
 MS. MABEL REBELLO: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India faces extreme shortage of health workers as per WHO 

218 
report; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that this shortage is impairing 
essential life- saving interventions i.e. childhood immunization, safe 
pregnancy and delivery service for mothers and access of treatment of 
HIV/AIDS, etc., and; 
(c) if so, what is the action plan of Government to address this 
issue? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c)  The  country  faces  acute  
shortage  of health workers at various  

219 
levels in the Public Health delivery system. The shortages reduce the 
range and quality of health services available to the citizens. The 
Government has undertaken several steps to remedy the situation and 
strengthen the delivery of health services in all the States. 
The Government has launched National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) on 
12th April 2005 for the period 2005- 2012 to provide accessible, 
affordable and quality health services to the poorest households in 
remotest rural regions of the country. 
The thrust of NRHM is on establishing a fully functional, community 
owned, decentralized health delivery system. The NRHM seeks to compensate 
various gaps through sector wide approach, enhanced funding, local untied 
and flexible funds and overall capacity building in the health system. 
Under NRHM, the community Health Worker called Accredited Social 
Health Activist (ASHA) has now been extended to entire country. This has 
substantially improved accessibility of health services for the citizens. 
Human resource augmentation is a key component of the National Rural 
Health Mission (NRHM). NRHM includes strategies like local recruitment of 
human resources on contract, recruitment for specific health facilities 
by the Rogi Kalyan Samitis, incentives and hard area allowances, blended 
payments to health functionaries for difficult areas, rational 
transfer/posting policies etc. The capacity for pre- service and in-
service trainings for critical skills has also been expanded under NRHM 
to address the availability and retention of key skills at health 
facilities. The successful implementation of NRHM has reduced the 
shortage of key health functionaries and improved availability of 
critical skills at public health facilities.

1322. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the World Bank's Global Monitoring Report 2008 has 
revealed rampant absenteeism among health workers in the country assessed 
at 40 per cent among the primary health care workers; 
(b) whether it is a fact that absenteeism among health workers is more 
acute in rural areas; and 
(c) whether this factor is likely to adversely impact the on- going 
Millennium Development Goals projects aimed at reducing child and 
maternal mortality? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) The world Bank's Global 
Monitoring Report 2008 has been published by World Bank (WB) and 
International Monitory Fund (IMF) as an assessment of progress made by 
various countries towards achieving the Millennium Development Goals 
(MGDs). The report is based on findings, interpretations and conclusions 
contained in working papers prepared by WB. The report notes that 
performance of health facilities in India can  be substantially improved 
if the absenteeism among health workers is addressed. 
Availability of appropriate skill mix at various levels in the public 
health delivery system is a key determinant of functionality of health 
facilities. Due to constraints of infrastructure and relatively weak 
overall development in rural areas, it has been a challenge to retain 
health functionaries on 24x7 basis in health facilities in rural areas. 
This factor has been noted as a key determinant to achieving the MDG in 

226 
India. 
To address this matter, the Government has included Human resource 
augmentation as key component of the National Rural Health Mission 
(NRHM). The NRHM was launched on 12th April 2005 for the period 2005- 2012 
and aims to provide accessible, affordable and quality health services to 
the poorest households in the remotest rural regions. NRHM includes 
strategies like local recruitment of human resources on contract, 
recruitment for specific health facilities by the Rogi Kalyan  Samitis,  
incentives  and  hard area  allowances, blended payments to health 
functionaries for  

227 
difficult areas, rational transfer/posting policies etc. The capacity for 
pre-service and in- service trainings for critical skills has also been 
expanded under NRHM to address the availability  and retention of key 
skills at health facilities. The successful implementation of NRHM has 
reduced absenteeism and improved availability of critical skills. This 
has accelerated the progress towards achievement of MDGs aimed at 
reducing child and maternal mortality.

FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether 53 per cent of children aged below five are without basic 
medical care than includes access to prenatal care, skilled child birth, 
immunization and treatment for diarrhea and pneumonia as per the latest 
data on child health care by a reputable global NGO– Save The Children; 
(b) if so, the details thereof;

first month of life in our country; and

this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) According to Save the Children, a 
US based Organisation, the State of the World's Mothers Report 2008, 
mentions that 53% per cent children under five do not have any access to 
health care. 
The sampling techniques, the methodology of sample collection and data 
survey have not been shared with the G overnment nor has the report been 
presented to the Government.

Health Survey-III (2005-06) of India 2006 is 39 per 1000 live births.

percentage of Basic Health Care Services being provided, are given in the 
Statement (See below). 
The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) (2005- 2012), and under its 
umbrella, the Reproductive and Child Health Programme Phase II, launched 
by the Government of India in the year 2005, aims to improve access to 
equitable, affordable, accountable and effective primary health care, in 
the rural areas of the country, especially for poor women and children, 
with a special focus on 18 States which have weak public health 
indicators and weak infrastructure. Strengthening of District Hospitals, 
Community Health centres Primary Health Care centres and Sub- centres to 
provide basic essential maternal and child health care. 
• Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), a cash benefit scheme to promote 
Institutional Delivery with a special focus on Below Poverty Line 
(BPL) and SC/ST pregnant women.

village to facilitate accessing of health care services by the 
community including pregnant women.

242 
(FRUs) and 50% of all Primary Health Centers for providing 24X7 
services.

skill-based trainings such as for providing Skilled Attendance at 
Birth.

Emergency Obstetric Care including Caesarian Section. 

243 
• Strengthening of District Hospitals, Community Health centres, Primary 
Health Care centres and Sub- centres to provide basic essential 
maternal and child health care. 
• Provision of 24 hours service in Primary Health Care centres and 
Skilled Attendance at Birth. 
• Strengthening of CHCs for first referral care - Provision of Emergency 
Obstetric and Neonatal Care at FRUs & Training of MBBS Doctors in Life 
Saving Anesthetics Skills for Emergency Obstetric Care. 
• Supplementary nutrition to pregnant and lactating mothers. 
• National nutrition anaemia prophylaxis programme. 
• Essential newborn care (care at birth -  protection from hypothermia -
provision of warmth, cord care -  protection from infection and early 
initiation of breastfeeding). 
• Immunisation. 
• Infant and young Child Feeding (Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months &

• Vitamin A+ supplementation.

children.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE

which are as under:- 
(i) prohibition of smoking in a public place; 
(ii) prohibition of direct and indirect advertisement; 
(ii) prohibition of sale of tobacco products to minors; 
(iv) prohibition of sale of tobacco products within 100 yards of

tobacco product packs.

Tobacco Control Programme (NTCP) in 18 Districts of 9 States during the 
year 2007-08. The programme broadly includes:

Tobacco Control Act, 2003;

Amendment of Organ Transplantation Act 
1345. DR. JANARDHAN WAGHMARE: 
 PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has been actively considering stringent 
amendments to the Organ Transplantation Act; 
(b) if so, the facts and details thereof; 
(c) whether illegal organ trade is still thriving in many parts of the 
country and the Organ Transplantation Act has completely failed to check 
such trade; and 
(d) if so, the steps taken by Government to check such illegal organ 
trade in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) The Honorable High Court of Delhi 
in CWP No. 813/2004 vide its order dated 06.09.2004 had set up a 
Committee to examine the provisions of Transplantation of Human Organs 
Act, 1994 and the Transplantation of Human Organs Rules, 1995. The report 
was submitted on 25.05.2005. A National Consultation was held on 

270 
18.05.2007 and the report was submitted in the second fortnight of August 
2007. The recommended changes required amendments in the Transplantation 
of Human Organs Act, 1994 (THOA) and the Rules framed thereunder.  
The amended Rules have been notified vide Gazetted Notification No. 
G.S.R.571(E) dated 04.08.08.  

271 
These changes are intended to facilitate genuine cases and to increase 
transparency in transplantation procedures. In so far as the Act is 
concerned the following amendments have been proposed: 
i) To allow swap operations between the related donor and recipients who 
do not match themselves but match with other similar 
donors/recipients. 
ii) To empower Union Territories, specially Government of NCT of Delhi 
to have their own appropriate authority instead of DGHS and/or 
Additional DG (Hospitals). 
iii) To make the punishments under the Act harsh and cognizable for the 
Illegal transplantation activities to deter the offenders from 
committing this crime. 
iv) To provide for registration of the centres for removal of organs 
from the cadavers and brain stem dead patients for harvesting of 
organs instead of registration of centres for transplantations only. 
Sale/purchase of human organs is already prohibited under 
Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994. Appropriate authorities 
established under this Act are responsible and empowered to check the 
illegal activities of human organs trafficking.

Empowering of girl child 
1349. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
 SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether country lost 30 million girls of foeticide and the Centre 
has decided to make Pre-natal Diagnostic Act more stringent; 
(b) if so, whether under proposed amendment to the Act clinics and 
doctors conducting sex determination would be stripped off their 

274 
licenses, fined up to Rs.7 lakh and be imprisoned for up to three years; 
(e) whether Prime Minister has urged every State to step forward 
towards empowering girl child; and 

275 
(d) to what extent the Union Government and the States have agreed to 
implement them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) The details containing the 
details of Child Sex Ratio (the number of girls per 1000 boys in the age 
group of 0-6 years) between 1971 and 2001 derived from the Census report 
is given in the Statement (See below). 
In order to check female foeticide, the Pre- natal Diagnostic 
Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994, was brought 
into operation from 1st January, 1996. The Pre- natal Diagnostic 
Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994 has since been 
amended to make it more comprehensive. The amended Act and Rules came 
into force with effect from 14.2.2003 and the PNDT Act has been renamed 
as "Pre- conception and Pre- Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of 
Sex Selection) Act, 1994" to make it more comprehensive. 
The technique of pre-conception sex selection has been brought within 
the ambit of this Act so as to pre- empt the use of such technologies, 
which significantly contribute to the declining sex ratio. Use of 
ultrasound machines has also been brought within the purview of this Act 
more explicitly so as to curb their misuse for detection and disclosure 
of sex of the foetus lest it should lead to female foeticide. The Central 
Supervisory Board (CSB) constituted under the Chairmanship of Minister 
for Health and Family Welfare has been further empowered for monitoring 
the implementation of the Act. State level Supervisory Boards in the line 
of the CSB constituted at the Centre has been introduced for monitoring 
and reviewing the implementation of the Act in States/UTs. The State/UT 
level Appropriate Authority has been made a multi member body for better 
implementation and monitoring of the Act in the States. More stringent 
punishments are prescribed under the Act so as to serve as a deterrent 
for minimizing violations of the Act. Appropriate Authorities are 
empowered with the powers of Civil Court for search, seizure and sealing 
the machines, equipments and records of the violators of law including 
sealing of premises and commissioning of witnesses. It has been made 
mandatory to maintain proper records in respect of the use of ultrasound 
machines and other equipments capable of detection of sex of foetus and 
also in respect of tests and procedures that may lead to pre-conception 
selection of sex. The sale of ultrasound machines has been regulated 

276 
through laying down the condition of sale only to the bodies registered 
under the Act. 
The proposal to amend the Act suitably with a view to making penalty 
provisions for violators of the Act more stringent, including imposition 
of fine up to Rs.5 lakhs and incarceration up to 7 years upon conviction, 
is being considered in consultation with legal experts and all the stake 
holders. 
The State/UT Governments have been requested to take forward the 
favourable impetus generated towards gild child on the occasion of the 
national level meet on 'Save the Girl Child, held at New Delhi on 
28.4.2008 and the message delivered by the hon'ble Prime Minister while 
inaugurating the meet in their respective States/UTs so that the age old 
bias against girl child is obliterated and the incidence of female 
foeticide is contained.

(a) whether it is a fact that many people are dying due to Chikungunya 
and Dengue all over the country especially in the agency areas of coastal 
Andhra Pradesh, particularly tribes; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) the steps to be taken to contain such diseases in each State and 
especially in Andhra Pradesh; and 

282 
(d) the number of death toll disease- wise in each State during the 
last three years, especially in Andhra Pradesh? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) No Sir. No deaths have been 
reported due to Chikungunya all over the country especially in the agency 
areas of coastal Andhra Pradesh, particularly tribes. 
In 2008 total 88974 clinically suspected cases were reported till 
November. Andhra Pradesh has reported 5 cases and Nil death. 
Dengue: In 2008, 79 deaths have been reported out of total 11488 cases 
till November. The case fatality rate has declined to 0.88% in 2008 from 
1.24% in 2007 and 1.49% in 2008. 
Andhra Pradesh has reported 273 cases and 2 deaths. Out of which 5 
cases and nil death were reported by Srikakulam district in agency areas 
of coastal Andhra Pradesh. 
(c) Government of India has taken following steps to contain such 
diseases in the country including Andhra Pradesh: 
• Prepared a strategic Action Plan for early case reporting & 
management, Entomological surveillance and anti mosquito measures for 
prevention and control of Dengue in the country and sent to the 
State(s) for implementation. 
• Guidelines on clinical management of dengue sent to the States. 
• Ensuring functioning of the 137 Sentinel Surveillance Hospitals (SSHs) 
and 13 Apex Referral Laboratories (ARLs) to facilitate the diagnostic 
facilities in the State(s) by providing IgM ELISA test kits for 
diagnosis of Dengue and Chikungunya including 10 Sentinel Surveillance 
Hospitals and 1 Apex Referral Laboratory in Andhra Pradesh. 
• IgM Mac ELISA test kits to all the SSHs and ARLs are being provided 
through National Institute of Virology, Pune. 
• Ensuring trained laboratory teams on sero- diagnosis of Dengue and 
Chikungunya in the identified institutes. 
• Endemic States have been requested to place rapid response teams at 
States and district Head Quarters to implement the remedial measures 
at the earliest on receipt of the report of any dengue or Chikungunya 
cases to prevent its further spread. 
• Availability of the guidelines for clinical management of Dengue/DHF 
cases sent to the State(s) for wider circulation. 
• State(s) were requested to prepare contingency plan for emergency 
hospitalization if any outbreak occurs. 
• In addition to regular supply of logistics like larvicides and 
adulticides cash grant is also being provided to the endemic State(s). 
• In 2006- 07 and 2007- 08 emergency package to the tune of Rs.21.60 
crores and Rs.8.75 crores have been released to the Chikungunya 
affected States to contain the disease. Out of which Rs.2.21 crores

2007-08 respectively. 
• Regular monitoring and periodic review is held to provide technical 
guidance to the affected State(s).

Health care in rural areas 
1360. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Reports submitted by various agencies 
like WHO and National Rural Health Mission have recommended for providing 
health care particularly in rural areas; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what are the steps Government is taking in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) The need for comprehensive 
improvements in health care delivery system particularly in Rural areas 
has been pointed out in several reports and forums. 
To address this need, the Government has launched National Rural 
Health Mission (NRHM) on 12th April 2005 for the period 2005- 2012. NRHM 
aims to provide accessible, affordable and accountable quality health 
services to the poorest households in the remotest rural regions. Under 
NRHM, 18 States including Bihar, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, 
Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Orissa and Rajasthan, eight North- East 
States, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir were classified as special 
focus States. 
The thrust of NRHM is on establishing a fully functional, community 
owned, decentralized health delivery system. NRHM facilitates 
simultaneous action on collateral determinants of health like water, 

294 
sanitation, education, nutrition, etc. Under NRHM Institutional 
integration has been carried out in the health sector and performance is 
benchmarked against Indian Public Health Standards. The NRHM seeks to 
compensate various gaps through enhanced funding, local untied and 
flexible funds and overall capacity building in the health system. 
NRHM has been operationalised in all the S tates in a decentralized 
manner on basis of Annual State Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs) 
which are appraised/approved by the national Programme Coordination 
Committee at Gol level.

1361. SHRI VIJAY JAWAHARLAL DARDA: 
 SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: 
Will the Minister of MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether pruning of reservation from 800 in 1997 to 114 till 2007 
for small scale sector, has in any  way, adversely affected the 
production capabilities of small and medium enterprises during the last 
decade; and 
(b) if not, whether his Ministry is proposing further pruning of items 
relating to stationery goods, electrical appliances, mechanical equipment 
and organic chemicals with twin objective of inviting additional players, 
domestic and foreign, into these areas to improve product quality and 
employment generation? 
THE MINISTER OF MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (SHRI MAHAVIR 
PRASAD): (a) The dereservation of products reserved for exclusive 
manufacture by micro and small enterprises (MSEs) has not had an overall 
adverse impact on MSEs, as concluded, inter alia, by the two empirical 
studies got conducted by the Government through Dalal Consultants and 
Engineers Ltd, and Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Contemporary Studies in the 
years 2001 and 2006 respectively. There is no policy of reservation of 
medium enterprises for exclusive manufacturing in that sector. 
(b) Items related to stationery goods, electrical appliances, organic 
chemicals and most of the items pertaining to mechanical equipment have 
since been dereserved. The issue of reservation and de-reservation of the 
items reserved for exclusive manufacture in MSE sector is examined on a 
continual basis by the Government, which takes into account the 
recommendations of the Advisory Committee constituted under the 
Industries (Development & Regulation) Act, 1951. These reviews consider 
various relevant aspects including inter alia, trends and development in 
external trade, domestic and global competitiveness, potential for 
employment and export, technical feasibility and economic viability of 
manufacture in the MSE sector etc.

THE MINISTER OF MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (SHRI MAHAVIR 
PRASAD): (a) to (c) For controlling the use of hazardous chemicals, 
including that by industry, the Government of India has notified the 
Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules, 1989 and 
Chemical Accident (Emergency, Planning, Preparedness and Response) Rules,

- Preparation of on-sight and off-sight emergency planning; 
- Preparation of safety reports and conduct safety audits;

- Report major accidents;

†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi

THE MINISTER OF MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (SHRI MAHAVIR 
PRASAD): (a) to (e) In the wake of recent global financial crisis, the 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) has been receiving 
representations from various Micro and Small Enterprises (MSB) 
Associations highlighting problems with regard to credit squeeze by the 
banks, high rates of interest on MSE loans, reduction in orders, delayed 
payments by the big enterprises, etc. While no specific information on 
job loss has been furnished, the Associations apprehend that if the 
present situation continues, it may lead to considerable lay- offs in the 
sector. 
The Government has announced on 7th December 2008 specific measures to 
support the MSME sector, which inter alia include: (i) extending 
guarantee cover under Credit Guarantee Scheme on loans from Rs.50 lakh to 
Rs.l crore with guarantee cover of 50 per cent and reducing lock- in

MSMEs; (iii) cut of 4 per cent in the ad valorem Cenvat rate for the 
balance part of current financial year on all products (other than 
petroleum and those where the current rate is less than 4 per cent) and 
(iv) interest subvention of 2 per cent in pre and post- shipment export 
credit for Small and Medium Enterprises (SME) sector upto 31st March 
2009. Further, the Reserve Bank of India has announced a refinance 
facility of Rs. 7,000 crore for Small Industries Development Bank of 
India (SIDBI) to facilitate the flow of credit to MSMEs.

than the ordinary staff in the Ministry of Railways after the 
implementation of recommendation of Sixth Central Pay Commission (CPC); 
and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the formula adopted for fixation of 
pay of running staff? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. VELU): (a) 
and (b) The revised pay in the pay band of running staff has been 
computed in the following manner : The existing basic pay as on 1.1.2006 
has been multiplied by a factor of 1.86 and the sum so arrived is added 
by an amount representing DA on the pay element @ 86% of 30% of existing 
basic pay. The resultant figure has been rounded off to next multiple of 
10. After determining the pay in the pay band in above manner, grade pay 
corresponding to the existing scale is payable. In case of other staff 
the pay in the pay band has been fixed simply by multiplying basic pay as 
on 01.01.2006 by a factor of 1.86. The dearness allowance to running 
staff is payable on basic pay and pay element of running allowance, while 
the same is payable to other employees on the basic pay alone. Due to 
this fact the revised basic pay of running staff at a particular stage in 
any specific existing (pre-revised) pay scale is generally higher than an 
ordinary staff at corresponding pre- revised stage & scale, after 
implementation of Sixth Central Pay Commission pay structure.

Steps to curb steel prices 
1392. SHRI JESUDASU SEELAM: Will the Minister of STEEL be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has taken serious steps to curb spiralling 
steel prices; 
(b) if so, whether Global Market Outlook (GMO) had taken stock of 
steel prices in the month of May; 
(c) if so, what steps have been taken by GMO in its meeting; and 
(d) to what extent Government has been able to curb spiralling steel 
prices and to what extent they have achieved? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI JITIN PRASADA): 
(a) Yes, Sir. The Government had taken the following measures between 
April-September 2008 to curb the spiralling steel prices: 
(i) DEPB on steel products was withdrawn w.e.f. 27.03.2008. 
(ii) Import Duty on all non-alloy steel, Zinc, ferro-alloys and metcoke 
was revised to 'Nil' from 5% w.e.f. 29.4.08. 
(iii) CVED on TMT bars and rounds was modified to 'Nil' from 14%.  
(iv) Export Duty on various categories of steel was imposed on 10.5.2008 

337 
and later enhanced on certain long products such as bars, wire rods, 
angles etc. w.e.f. 13.06.08. 
(v) Ad-valorem export duty of 15% was imposed on iron ore of all 
categories and grades w.e.f. 13.06.2008. 

338 
(b) and (c) Ministry of Steel is not associated with Global Market 
Outlook and has no information to furnish in this regard. 
(d) The various steps taken by Government in improving steel 
availability in the domestic market through retailers and dealers brought 
about price stability in the market. The retail price of steel in the 
domestic market was Rs.8,000- Rs. 10,000 lower than the international 
price, as a result of various positive fiscal and administrative steps 
taken by the government and continued to be stable between July and 
September 2008. 
Imposition of duty on import of steel 
1393. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the steel industry is undergoing a very 
rough phase after the melt down in the global economy; 
(b) if so, whether the steel producers have sought imposition of 15% 
duty on import of steel and other measures to survive; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the reaction of Government in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI JITIN PRASADA): 
(a) As a result of global financial crises, the demand for steel has 
become sluggish. The rate of steel consumption growth has come down to 
1.1% during April- November 2008 against 2.4% during April- October 2008 
and 4.9% during April-September 2008. 
(b) and (c) Ministry of Steel has received a large number of 
representations from steel industry and industry associations regarding 
sudden fall in steel demand, sharp decline in international steel prices; 
and requesting the Government to take appropriate fiscal measures to 
avoid cheap imports of steel into the country. In order to safeguard the 
domestic steel industry Government has imposed 5% import duty on steel 
w.e.f., 18.11.2008. Further, Government has withdrawn the duty on export 
of all steel items w.e.f., 31.10.2008, restored DEPB benefit on steel 
export w.e.f., 14.11.2008 put the import of Hot Rolled Coils in the 
restricted list of imports w.e.f., 21.11.2008 and also reduced Excise 
Duty on steel items from 14% to 10% w.e.f. 7.12.2008.
